title: Guinness World Record Mom Jenn Drummond on Ambition & Identity
guestBio: Jenn Drummond is a mountaineer, entrepreneur, author, and mother of seven who made history on June 1, 2023, when Guinness World Records recognized her as the first woman to complete the Second Seven Summits (Bass-version). Her journey began after a near-fatal car accident forced her to confront the ambitions she had quietly been postponing. She is also the host of the Take a Break with Jenn podcast and a passionate advocate for women choosing goals that belong entirely to them.
excerpt: After a car accident forced her to reckon with her "someday" list, mother of seven Jenn Drummond became the first woman to complete the Second Seven Summits — earning a Guinness World Record. In this conversation with Aimee Rickabus, Jenn unpacks the good-girl roles she left behind, what mountains teach about leadership, and the question every woman needs to ask herself.
metaDescription: Guinness World Record holder Jenn Drummond joins Aimee Rickabus to talk ambition, motherhood, and leaving the good-girl role behind. Ep. 86 of The Manage Her®.
keyTakeaways: A life-altering moment — like a car accident — can be the clarifying force that turns vague 'someday' dreams into concrete, committed goals you actually pursue.
Leaving behind the 'good girl' role isn't an act of selfishness; it's an act of integrity that allows you to show up more fully for yourself and the people who love you.
The truest test of a goal is whether you would still chase it without an audience — if the answer is yes, you've found something worth your energy.
Letting your children watch you pursue something difficult and personal is one of the most powerful forms of leadership you can model for them.
Knowing when to turn around — choosing people over peaks — is not failure; it is wisdom, and it reflects the same discernment that makes great leaders.
Building an ambitious life requires real, practical support, and asking for help is not a weakness but a prerequisite for doing hard things sustainably.
Ordinary Tuesdays are where life actually happens, and bringing small, intentional moments of meaning to them is just as important as chasing the summit.

pullQuotes.text: Would you still do it without the applause? That's the question that tells you everything about whether a goal is really yours.
I didn't have to be good at classroom glue projects. That wasn't my mountain. I had to figure out what was.
Turning around isn't quitting. Knowing when people matter more than the peak — that's the real summit.
Fear can ride along. You don't have to wait until it's gone to start moving.
Someday is a lie we tell ourselves. You have to put a date on it or it doesn't exist.

quiz.title: What Kind of Mountain Climber Are You?
quiz.description: You don't have to summit a peak to have a mountain worth climbing. This self-discovery quiz — inspired by Jenn Drummond's conversation with Aimee Rickabus — helps you understand how you relate to ambition, permission, and the goals you've been quietly carrying. Answer honestly. There are no wrong answers here.

A.name: The Visionary Trailblazer
A.description: You've always had a vivid sense of what's possible — for you, for your people, for the world around you. You're the one who sees the summit before anyone else has thought to look up. The challenge for you isn't imagination; it's giving yourself full permission to commit without waiting for consensus. Jenn's episode will remind you that the goal that feels too big is often exactly the right size — and that the applause question will help you know for certain.

B.name: The Steadfast Nurturer
B.description: You lead through love, and the people around you feel it. You are deeply attuned to what others need, and you give generously — sometimes at the quiet expense of your own dreams. Jenn's story speaks directly to you: your ambition is not a threat to the people you care for. Letting them see you pursue something that is fully yours is one of the greatest gifts you can give them. This episode will give you language for the both/and you've been afraid to claim.

C.name: The Grounded Pragmatist
C.description: You believe in doing the work, building the plan, and making things actually happen. You're not one for lofty inspiration that doesn't connect to real action — and you're right to be skeptical. What you'll find in Jenn's conversation is exactly that: the practical, honest, unglamorous side of living ambitiously, including the team it takes, the moments of turning around, and the small Tuesday intentions that add up to something extraordinary. This episode is built for the way your mind works.

D.name: The Evolving Seeker
D.description: You are in the middle of becoming — and you know it. Something has shifted, or is shifting, and you're in that in-between place where the old role no longer fits but the new one isn't fully formed yet. Jenn's journey from 'good girl' to Guinness World Record holder is a map through exactly that terrain. This episode will meet you where you are and remind you that the most important climb is the one toward the person you're choosing to become.

questions.question: When you imagine a big, personal goal, what's your most honest first reaction?

options.text: Excitement — I can already picture the path forward.
Warmth followed by worry — I wonder how it would affect the people I love.
Curiosity — I want to know if it's actually doable before I get attached.
A strange mix of longing and uncertainty — I'm not sure who I'd be if I really went for it.

questions.question: If no one in your life would ever know about a goal you achieved, how would that change your motivation?

options.text: It wouldn't — I'd still want it just as much, maybe more.
It would be harder — sharing the journey with people I love is part of what makes it meaningful.
It would sharpen my focus — I'd want to make sure the outcome itself was worth it.
It might actually be freeing — without the audience, I could figure out what I truly want.

questions.question: How do you tend to handle a moment when the 'right' choice and the 'ambitious' choice feel like they're in conflict?

options.text: I look for the creative third option that doesn't make me choose.
I usually lean toward what's best for the people around me, then revisit my own needs.
I assess the tradeoffs clearly and make the most logical call I can.
I sit with the discomfort for a while — I'm still figuring out how to weigh my own needs.

questions.question: When you think about the roles you play every day — mother, professional, partner, friend — how do they feel?

options.text: Energizing, but I sometimes wish I had even more space to lead and create.
Deeply meaningful — they're the core of who I am, even when they're exhausting.
Manageable — I work hard to be effective in each one and keep things running well.
A little constricting lately — I'm wondering what else is part of my identity.

questions.question: What does asking for help feel like for you?

options.text: Natural — I know I need a strong team to do anything worth doing.
Easier when it's for someone else — much harder when the help is for my own goals.
Fine, as long as I've done everything I can on my own first.
Uncomfortable — I'm still learning to believe my goals are worth other people's support.

questions.question: There's something on your 'someday' list you've been quietly carrying. What's kept it there?

options.text: The timing hasn't felt quite right — I'm waiting for the right window to commit.
I'm not sure it's fair to pursue it when others need so much from me right now.
I haven't built out a realistic plan yet, and I won't start until I have one.
Honestly, I'm not sure I'm ready to know who I am if I actually go after it.

content:
There is a version of your life you keep tucking into the back of a drawer, labeled someday. You know the one. The goal that feels too big, too selfish, or too far outside the role you've agreed to play. Jenn Drummond knows that drawer well — and she's here to tell you it's time to open it.

In Episode 86 of The Manage Her® Podcast, Aimee Rickabus sits down with Jenn Drummond, the first woman in history to complete the Second Seven Summits (Bass-version) — a feat recognized by Guinness World Records on June 1, 2023. But the most important part of Jenn's story didn't happen on a mountain. It happened in a car.

The Accident That Rewrote the Timeline

Before the summits, before the record, Jenn was doing what a lot of high-functioning women do: excelling at the roles assigned to her. She was good at being good. Then a near-fatal car accident interrupted everything and asked her a question she couldn't outrun — if your time is finite, what are you actually doing with it?

That question cracked open her someday list. Not the one she'd been curating for other people's approval, but the private one. The goals she'd filed away because they felt too ambitious, too inconvenient, or too hard to justify. The accident didn't give her permission to dream — it made her stop asking for permission at all.

The Good-Girl Role Nobody Asked You to Audition For

One of the most honest threads in this conversation is Jenn's willingness to name the "good girl" role she had been playing — and to describe what it actually cost her. She wasn't a bad mother or a disengaged woman. She was doing everything right. And that was exactly the problem. Because doing everything right, by someone else's definition, meant she was slowly disappearing from her own life.

She tells Aimee she had to reckon with the truth that she was not the classroom-glue-project mother — and that was okay. Her mountain wasn't a craft table. Yours might not be either. The freedom in this conversation is that Jenn never tells you what your mountain should be. She just refuses to let you pretend you don't have one.

Motherhood, Ambition, and the Both/And

Jenn is a mother of seven. She did not climb the Second Seven Summits despite that — she climbed them with it, in full view of her children. This is one of the most powerful reframes in the episode: your ambition is not something you pursue in spite of your family. It is something your family gets to witness. And that witnessing matters.

When her children watch her choose something difficult and pursue it anyway — when they see her plan, prepare, struggle, and ultimately stand on a summit — they are receiving a lesson that no classroom can teach. They are learning that their mother is a full person. That full people chase things. And that they are allowed to be full people too.

Jenn also speaks honestly about the grief that can accompany a new season of motherhood — the particular ache of children growing up and needing you differently. That grief, she says, can either be the thing that holds you still or the thing that propels you toward who you are becoming. She chose propulsion.

Turning Around Is Not the Same as Quitting

One of the most quietly radical moments in this conversation comes when Jenn talks about turning around before reaching a summit. In a culture obsessed with finishing, with grinding through, with the motivational poster version of never giving up — Jenn offers something more nuanced and more true. Sometimes turning around is the right call. Sometimes the people waiting at home are the actual summit.

This is the kind of leadership wisdom that doesn't fit on a coffee mug. It requires judgment, not just grit. It requires knowing what you're climbing for, not just what you're climbing toward. And it reframes what success actually looks like when you're living a full, complicated, beautiful life and not just optimizing a metric.

The Applause Question That Changes Everything

At the center of this episode is a question Aimee and Jenn return to again and again: Would you still do it without the applause? It sounds simple. It is not simple. It is the question that separates goals you've borrowed from goals that are actually yours. It is the question that separates performance from purpose.

Jenn's answer, when she held it up to her climbing, was yes — and that yes is what carried her through the hard parts. When you find a goal your answer is yes to, you stop needing external validation to keep moving. That's not a small thing. That is one of the most liberating shifts a woman can make.

The Team Behind the Dream

Jenn is also refreshingly honest about what made her record possible: real, practical help. She does not pretend she did this alone. She talks about the infrastructure behind her family life, the people who made it possible for her to be on a mountain while also being a present mother of seven. Asking for help is not a footnote in her story. It is a chapter.

This matters because the myth of the woman who does it all, alone, without systems or support, is not inspiring — it's isolating. Jenn's story invites you to build the team, ask the question, make the arrangement, and stop treating self-sufficiency as the price of admission to an ambitious life.

Your Mountain Is Waiting

You don't need climbing boots to take something home from this conversation. You need the willingness to ask yourself what you've been filing under someday and what it would take to give it a date instead. Jenn Drummond stood on the top of a Guinness World Record — and the question she brings back down is one you can use on an ordinary Tuesday, in the middle of a regular life, without leaving your zip code.

What do you want to do with the life in front of you? That's your mountain. This episode will help you start climbing.
